claims.text: The WTaTiVZr alloy is processed by powder metallurgy with a fine TiC dispersion.
Fine TiC particles act as barriers to dislocation motion at high temperature.
TiC-mediated inhibition of dislocation motion enhances plastic strain and toughness relative to pure tungsten.
The dispersed TiC particles interact with and pin dislocations in the HEA matrix.
Dislocation impediment by TiC causes stress redistribution.
Dislocation impediment by TiC activates secondary slip systems.
Stress redistribution and activation of secondary slip systems delay crack initiation and propagation.
Under identical high-temperature loading, the TiC-dispersed HEA will exhibit greater plastic strain than pure tungsten.
Under identical high-temperature loading, the TiC-dispersed HEA will absorb more energy before failure than pure tungsten.
The TiC-dispersed HEA will show increased yield strain relative to pure tungsten.
The TiC-dispersed HEA will show delayed crack growth relative to pure tungsten.
The proposed enhancement is limited to high-temperature loading relevant to plasma-facing applications.
The enhancement may not occur at lower temperatures or after processing routes that do not produce a uniform TiC dispersion.
Prior studies suggest that TiC dispersions improve ductility in tungsten-based systems.
The magnitude of the improvement depends on TiC particle uniformity and size distribution.

contradictions.description: The comparison changes both the matrix composition and the presence of TiC: WTaTiVZr plus TiC is compared with pure W without TiC. It therefore cannot isolate TiC dispersion as the hypothesized cause, despite the baseline being described as isolating the effect. A factorial comparison including WTaTiVZr with and without TiC would be required to isolate TiC.
